resources.string: Forwards touch events from the LSFG overlay to the underlying app so you can interact with games while the frame-generation overlay is visible.

Follow these steps to get the most out of frame generation. Tap any screenshot to view it full size.
Tutorial content will be added soon. Drop your screenshots in res/drawable-nodpi and reference them in TutorialScreen.kt.

Welcome to LSFG-Android! It is strongly recommended to read the tutorial before using the app — it walks you through accessibility permissions, loading Lossless.dll, picking a target app and the overlay menu.\n\nYou can always reopen the tutorial later from the Tutorial entry on the home screen.
Choose how to open the in-game settings panel: a draggable floating icon, or a swipe-from-edge drawer.

On some devices the edge-swipe drawer may not respond, leaving you stuck on the overlay with no way to close it from inside the game. The floating icon is the recommended option. Continue with the drawer?

Hosts the overlay as a trusted accessibility surface so taps reach the app underneath on strict devices (e.g. Orange Pi 5 Ultra) where they would otherwise be blocked. Trade-off: while a session is running the overlay covers the status bar and navigation bar — you cannot pull down notifications or tap home/back. Leave OFF if your device passes taps already; turn ON only when you cannot tap through. Requires the LSFG accessibility service to be enabled.
MediaProjection captures through Android screen sharing. Shizuku and Root capture use a privileged UID-filtered target capture path, useful on devices whose MediaProjection includes overlays.

Hides the framegen overlay while your finger is on the screen for zero-latency touch response, and resumes ~0.25s after release. Intended for browsing and video apps; leave off for games. Exact with Shizuku/Root; approximate (resume timer) with MediaProjection.
Show a live plot of generated frame intervals in the overlay. Useful for diagnosing stutter.
Number of frames produced per real frame. 2 = one interpolated frame between each pair. 3–4 recommended on mobile.
Internal motion estimation resolution. Lower = faster but less accurate.
Use the faster, lower-quality shader variant. Recommended on mid-range GPUs.
Enable only if your device and game output HDR.
Suppress generated frames during very fast camera movement to reduce missing character parts and warping. Off by default.

Use the half-precision shader variants pre-compiled inside Lossless.dll instead of the full-precision DXBC set. Reduces GPU load and memory bandwidth. Quality is virtually identical; falls back to FP32 automatically if anything goes wrong.
Runs a handcrafted NNAPI graph (unsharp-mask, detail boost, chroma clean, game crisp) entirely on the dedicated accelerator. Device: %1$s
Disabled because Android does not report a dedicated NNAPI accelerator. Device: %1$s
Strength of the enhance kernel. Higher values give a crisper image but can exaggerate compression artifacts.
Blur radius used by the unsharp-mask paths. Larger radius brings out broader edges; smaller radius targets fine detail.
1x keeps output size; 2x requests NPU bilinear upscale before the enhance pass.
Pure CPU pixel pass applied after the NPU stage. Cheap, always available, and tunable with saturation, vibrance and vignette on top of the preset.
Primary amount controlling the current CPU preset (contrast boost, sharpen amount, cinematic mix, …).
Zero desaturates the frame; 50 percent is neutral; full pushes colors toward vivid.
Lifts low-saturation pixels without over-boosting already vivid ones. Useful for grayed-out HUDs and skin tones.
Darkens the corners on a cosine falloff starting at 60% of the radius.
Use Vulkan GPU post-processing methods for image upscaling and enhancement.
Controls the requested output scale for methods that upscale.
Controls the intensity of non-scale enhancement passes.
Show a small FPS readout in the top-left of the overlay. MediaProjection counts visible capture frames; Shizuku capture counts privileged UID-filtered target frames.
Choose where the in-game drawer handle appears on the overlay.
Pick the game or app you want to apply frame generation to. It will be launched when you start the session.
Pick the apps that should automatically show the LSFG launcher when opened from the home screen. A small floating icon appears on top of the game; tap it to start the frame-generation overlay.
Enable the LSFG accessibility service so the app can detect when one of the selected games is opened.
Disable Automatic Overlay for this app
Tap to start the LSFG capture session for this app. Android will ask you to confirm screen recording.
The overlay permission is required. Please grant "Display over other apps".
Screen capture was denied. LSFG cannot run without it.
Optional. LSFG renders at full opacity and forwards touches to the game without this service. Enable it only if you notice rendering issues on a specific device.
A report was saved. You can share it with the developer to help debug the issue. Device and extension info is already included — no personal data is attached.
No diagnostic log available yet — run a session first.
Runs three back-to-back passes (multiplier ×2, ×3, ×4) with a fixed preset and produces a shareable report. Use this baseline before/after performance changes to measure deltas.
Flow scale 0.70 · Performance mode ON · Anti-artifacts OFF · Post-processing OFF · Vsync AUTO
Each run: 60 seconds sampling + 2 seconds warmup. Total ~3 minutes plus target-app launch.
FP16 supported on this GPU — the benchmark will run twice (FP32 then FP16) for direct side-by-side numbers in the same report.
Pick a target app first (in the Automatic Overlay screen).
Report saved to %1$s. Use the share sheet to send it.
No report available yet — run a benchmark first.

Accessibility is off. LSFG is probing the foreground app in the background via Shizuku/Root and shows the launcher icon when a selected app is opened. Lock LSFG in Recents so the system does not kill the background service.
Target entered a small window — session ended
LSFG overlay dot needs the “Display over other apps” permission. Please allow it in system settings.
The floating dot and the frame-generation overlay both rely on the “Display over other apps” permission. It is not granted yet, so the dot cannot appear.
Ready for Shizuku capture. Frames are captured straight from the target UID and the LSFG overlay is never fed back into itself.
Ready for root capture. Frames are captured from the target UID with root privileges — no screen-recording dialog.
Ready. When Android asks what to share, pick the target app — not the entire screen.
Complete steps 1 and 2 below to start a session.

Smooth — steadiest picture, best for video and slow-paced games; slightly slower response. Low latency — the most responsive input, best for fast shooters/action games; occasional stutter when frame rate fluctuates. Balanced — the middle ground; pick this for most scenarios.
Master switch for frame generation. Off = raw capture passthrough (no interpolation).
Pacing controls when generated frames are delivered — presets, VSync alignment and the FPS cap. Full pacing tuning lives in the in-game overlay menu (advanced EMA/slack/queue sliders).
Changes take effect when the next session starts. While a session is running, open the in-game drawer to tweak values live.
The floating dot stays on every app and the launcher; open its panel to toggle frame generation for whatever is in front.
Both the floating dot and the frame-generation overlay need “Display over other apps”. Tap to open system settings.
Pick Lossless.dll from the install folder of your own Steam copy of Lossless Scaling.
Real %1$s fps · Posted %2$s fps (latency %3$s ms · queue %4$s ms)
Manual changes switch the preset to Custom. Misconfiguration may reduce smoothness.

LSFG-Android needs the accessibility permission to drive the overlay and frame generation correctly. You can open the device accessibility settings straight from the system Settings app, or tap the accessibility icon in the top-right corner of the LSFG-Android home screen.
Find and tap “LSFG Touch Passthrough” in the accessibility services list.
Turn on the LSFG-Android accessibility switch as shown in the screenshot.

If the switch won’t turn on, your device is likely restricting sideloaded apps via Restricted settings. Open the LSFG-Android App info page and look at the top-right — you will see a menu icon (red box in the screenshot). Tap it and enable the option that appears (usually “Allow restricted settings”). Then go back and repeat the previous step — the accessibility switch will now turn on.
From the home screen tap “Select DLL”, then choose the Lossless.dll file from your own copy of Lossless Scaling.

Read the legal notice carefully. Using this app requires that you own a Steam copy of Lossless Scaling — the Lossless.dll you load must come from your own copy. The DLL is not, and never will be, bundled with this app.
Use the system file picker to select Lossless.dll from your Lossless Scaling copy.
Once the DLL has been processed you will land on this page — shaders are extracted and ready to use.
To choose which app gets frame generation, open item 2 in the main menu — “Target apps”.
You will see every app and game installed on the device. Use the search bar to find the target quickly, then tap it to set it as the frame-generation target.
This section holds every setting related to the LSFG overlay and how it is displayed on screen.

This setting controls how the overlay menu opens during a session. The default is an icon button: tap it during a session to open the live settings drawer. You can also switch to a slide-in drawer (drag from the screen edge toward the center). Warning: drawer mode is unreliable on some Android devices and may leave you unable to open the menu or even dismiss the overlay. If that happens you may need to reboot to recover icon mode. The icon button is recommended.
If your device supports the drawer, use this setting to choose which edge it docks to (left, right, top, bottom).
Here you can enable the on-screen FPS counter and the frame pacing graph. Note: these readings are best-effort estimates and may not be 100%% accurate.

This option hosts the overlay via the accessibility service instead of a regular system overlay window. If the standard overlay misbehaves on your device, try this — it is more resilient against aggressive vendor background killing.

Choose between MediaProjection capture (default) and Shizuku-assisted capture. If you already tried MediaProjection — including toggling the accessibility-hosted overlay in the previous step — and the overlay still does not work, switch to Shizuku as a fallback.
This section gathers all settings that control frame-generation behaviour.

These are the settings I consider optimal on top-end devices such as the Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5 — optical flow scaling can safely be set to 1 on such chips. Even on flagships I recommend the LSFG performance variant over the standard one. Anti-artifact mode is still experimental and not recommended.
Once everything is configured, tap “Start LSFG session” to launch both the target app and the frame-generation overlay.
Some Android devices will now show a screen-sharing picker. When it appears, choose to share only the target app you selected in LSFG-Android — not the whole screen.
The target app will start with the LSFG overlay running on top of it, and frame generation takes effect.
If you picked the icon button in settings, it sits on one side of the screen during a session — tap it to open the overlay menu.
If you picked the drawer, it sits on the screen edge you chose. To open the overlay menu, drag the drawer from the edge toward the center of the screen.
These are all the options in the overlay menu — every parameter listed can be adjusted live during a session.
